items.title: Prawn masala and spiced roast cauliflower: Romy Gill’s Indian recipes for chilly nights
items.summary:
Spiced prawns cooked in coconut milk and a whole roast cauliflower with almonds and coriander – these dishes take me back to the food of my childhood

These two dishes are just the kind of food I want to eat on a chilly evening. The cauliflower is deeply spiced, nutty and comforting, with coconut, almonds, ginger and chilli bringing warmth and texture, while the prawn masala is quicker and lighter, but still full of flavour, with the spices and the sweet prawns coming together beautifully. Both dishes reflect the way I love to cook: generous, vibrant with layers of spice, but never so much that you lose the character of the main ingredient.

items.summary:
You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

Buttermilk Pie 

Tracy Mulder, Allrecipes 

Since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor

items.title: The Best Holiday Cocktails, According to Eater Editors
items.summary:
In the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic , totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch. 

Now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Consider this your cheat sheet for next time you’re asked to bring something tasty to the party | Eater Staff 

There’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests. 

Granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

items.title: Help! Why does my apple pie always have a soggy base? | Kitchen aide
items.summary:
Direct the heat and minimise the moisture to save your pastry from a saturated bottom, says our panel of pie pros

Why does the pastry base of my apple pie always come out soggy? What am I doing wrong?
Sophie, by email
“The very first thing I would say is that Sophie has got to look at her filling, and how wet it is,” says Calum Franklin, author of The Modern Pie Maker and all-round pie Yoda. “Apples contain quite a lot of water already, so you don’t generally need to add any extra liquid to the filling.” Instead, he’d simply cook the apples with sugar: “Just let them break down.”

That said, Sophie could always consider including some sort of barrier, too, says Dee Rettali, co-founder of Fortitude Bakehouse in London: “My mother was an amazing baker, and she always sprinkled a very fine crumble mix [just sugar and flour, no fat] on the bottom of her pie before putting in any fruit. That will then absorb most of the liquid.”

Got a culinary dilemma? Email feast@theguardian.com

items.title: Where Chef Esther Choi Eats on Her Day Off in NYC
items.summary:
Celebrity chef and cookbook author Esther Choi, the chef behind Korean restaurants like mǒkbar and Ms. Yoo , shows us the cafe, bakery, and restaurants she visits weekly for everything from taro-mochi doughnuts to soup dumplings.

Choi starts her day with co-fermented coffee at Tera Espresso Bar , where all the beans are roasted in-house and signatures are co-fermented with fruits. She grabs her coffee made with beans that were fermented with tangerines and heads to pastry chef Dominique Ansel’s bakery, Papa D’Amour . Ansel shows her how he makes his labor-intensive taro-mochi doughnut that is filled with a strawberry jam and frozen before being fried up. Next is the viral butter-dipped vanilla soft serve that Choi gets to dip in the warm butter herself.

Choi then heads to NYC icon Pastis for lunch, ordering the cheese-crusted French onion soup, fries, and a dirty martini. The deeply flavorful French onion soup takes four hours to make. Choi recommends ordering your own — this is not a dish you’ll want to share. Her super briny vodka martini hits the table as Choi reminisces about working at Food Network nearby and coming to Pastis with co-workers.

For her final spot, Choi heads to Pinch Chinese in Soho for her favorite soup dumplings in the city. Her son Leon and husband Josh join her for dinner, digging into pork soup dumplings, Peking duck, steak fried rice, and pea shoots. Of course, two-year-old Leon already knows exactly how to slurp a soup dumpling.

Watch the most recent episode of Chef’s Day Off to see how chef Esther Choi spends her day off at her favorite…

items.title: How a New Restaurant Injected Retro “Latin Soul” Into a New-Build Space
items.summary:
This excerpt was originally published in Pre Shift, our newsletter for the hospitality industry. Subscribe for more first-person accounts, advice, and interviews .

Opened at the end of October, Bar Nuestro is Washington, D.C.’s newest bistro serving European- and Latin-inspired dishes and drinks. Founder Daniella Senior and designer Shawn Hausman ( whose firm worked on iconic spaces like the Chateau Marmont and the ’80s club Area ) collaborated on the project, ensuring that the space captured the same retro vibe as the menu. I especially hope their mini-private-dining room concept catches on.

Pre Shift: Tell me about the design concept for Bar Nuestro. 

Daniella Senior: We wanted the space to really feel—even though it’s a new buildout—that it’s been there a long time. I’m kind of tired of the same aesthetic going around, one that’s almost too clean, too new, too matchy-matchy. I think that doesn’t, at times, help you communicate what the food is trying to communicate. For us, the food and the space work together. We wanted it to feel very Old World. We took a lot of inspiration from Vienna’s old corner cafes, which have been institutions for a while. We wanted a “We’ve been here a minute” type of feel. 

From our furniture to our tiles, [the Bar Nuestro team and designer Shawn Hausman] sourced a lot of vintage pieces, about 25 percent of the furniture. We have chairs that came from Austria and Italy in the ’30s and fabric with vintage patterns. When Shawn was traveling through Europe, he’d send pictures of things he found, and I sourced accent pieces—like the credenza…

items.summary:
Slow-cooked pork in a deliciously sweet-salty glaze is Vietnamese comfort food at its best

Many moons ago, I attended a cookery class in Hanoi that revealed to me the glories of thịt kho tàu, a simple but unbelievably delicious dish of caramelised pork braised in sweet coconut water and savoury fish sauce, enlivened by plenty of black pepper. In fact, loved it so much that I put their version in my cookbook, The A to Z of Eating, and then somehow forgot all about it for a decade. It’s easy to do that when you’re always working on the next recipe, but this week has been a very welcome rediscovery, not least because I’ve learned a lot more about what chef Thuy Diem Pham describes in her book The Little Viet Kitchen as “the ultimate home comfort food”.

A family favourite, it’s also traditionally served as part of the lunar new year celebrations, because, in the words of Andrea Nguyen, “Tet is for savouring abundance, which explains why this rich, savoury braise of pork and eggs in bittersweet caramel sauce is a must-have”; and also, according to blogger Hungry Huy, “because of how well it keeps after cooking”. items.title: Blacklock, Birmingham B3: ‘A very, very cool version of an Angus Steakhouse’ – restaurant review
items.summary:
Ever-open, eminently relatable, sensibly priced spots of this sort will always have an audience

A London chophouse has taken up residence on St Philip’s Place, Birmingham, on the edge of Cathedral Square, or “Pigeon Park”, as the locals call it. This particular nook of Brum city centre is a magnet to those feathered blighters, although Blacklock’s smoulderingly macho menu is ironically pigeon-meat free, revolving instead around heaps of chops and steaks cooked over charcoal. There’s porterhouse, bone-in sirloin, lamb rump and pig’s head on toast.

Launched in London in 2015, Blacklock was the elegant, edgy, no-nonsense dining experience for groovy young things who quite literally wanted meat and two veg, so long as said veg was dripping-fat chips; it now has five sites in the capital and another in Manchester. “We just ended up at Blacklock,” people used to tell me half a dozen times a week, then go on to rave about the bread, the gravy and the ash-baked sweet potatoes, and revel in the glorious simplicity of it all. Modern life was complex, Blacklock was not, but neither was it cheap enough to feel like a jaunt down the Toby Carvery. And now its big flavours and broad appeal have hit the UK’s second city.
